en.title: Islamic Law: the whole course
en.short: An academic guide to Islamic law: sources, schools, main areas, study methods and common pitfalls.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text:
These notes are for learning, not legal advice. Islamic law is not a single code. It is a family of juristic traditions, and its application differs by country, court and community. A rule stated here may be a majority view in one school, a statute in one country, or a practice in one region. Do not rely on these notes for a real case. Speak to a qualified lawyer or mufti in your country.

Always ask which country and which school or statute a rule comes from. Check the current official text of any statute, and the current fatwa of any institution you cite. Where the notes mention Nigeria, Malaysia or another country, the rule belongs to that country only.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Islamic law is the body of rules and reasoning that Muslims regard as derived from divine guidance and developed by jurists. Two terms are often distinguished. Shari’ah is the broader revealed path. Fiqh is the human understanding of that path: the jurists’ rulings, with differences of opinion. Fiqh is not the same as a modern state statute, though many states codify parts of it.

The subject studies primary sources (the Qur’an and the Sunnah), secondary sources and reasoning (ijma, qiyas, ijtihad), and the schools of law. It also studies usul al-fiqh (legal theory), legal maxims, maqasid (objectives), and the historical development of the law. It is academic study, not a ruling on anyone’s faith.

sections.heading: How the course is usually organised
sections.text:
Islamic law is taught in several routes. In Nigeria, it is usually studied within the LLB, with courses on Islamic law, and also in Shari’ah programmes. To appear in Sharia courts, graduates need the qualifications that the relevant state and federal rules require, so check the current rules. In Malaysia, syariah law degrees and syariah court practice form a separate route from civil law. In Saudi Arabia, Islamic law is often the core of the law degree. In many other countries it is an elective or a postgraduate specialism.

Length and awards differ by country and institution. A law degree may take three, four or five years. A master’s (LLM or MA) usually takes one or two years and includes a dissertation. Check your own faculty handbook for the current structure, core courses and professional requirements.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory courses build the foundation. They cover Shari’ah and fiqh, the Qur’an and Sunnah, ijma, qiyas and ijtihad, the schools of law, usul al-fiqh, legal maxims and maqasid, historical development, the division between ibadat (worship) and muamalat (transactions), and the authority of fatwa.

Core courses apply this to fields: marriage and divorce, maintenance and custody, inheritance and wills, waqf, contracts and sale, riba and Islamic finance, property, criminal law (hudud, qisas, ta’zir), evidence and procedure, constitutional thought (siyasah), human rights, international law (siyar), Islamic law in Nigeria, legal pluralism and comparative law, ethics and adab, and codification and reform.

Master’s courses go deeper: advanced usul and contemporary ijtihad, Islamic finance regulation, biomedical ethics, and research methods for a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the Arabic terms early and use them precisely. For each rule, note the source, the school, the country and the statute or case if there is one. Read a translation of the Qur’an alongside a recognised commentary, and check the grading of any hadith before you rely on it.

For problem questions, use a simple method. State the issue. State the rule and its authority. Apply it to the facts. Give a conclusion. Say where the schools differ and why. Do not issue a fatwa; describe the reasoning.

Compare countries and schools. Keep a table of terms, sources and differences. Write short summaries from memory, then check them.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Treating fiqh as one unchanging code. It is a juristic tradition with internal disagreement.

Confusing Shari’ah with fiqh, or a state statute with divine law.

Ignoring the school. A Hanafi rule may differ from a Maliki or Ja’fari rule.

Citing a hadith without checking its authenticity or its context.

Assuming a Nigerian statute or court structure applies in Malaysia or Saudi Arabia.

Giving personal opinion as law, or answering a real dispute instead of explaining the law.

Forgetting to check whether a statute or fatwa is still current.

keyPoints: These notes are for learning, not legal advice, and Islamic law is not a single code.
Shari’ah is the revealed path; fiqh is the jurists’ human understanding of it.
Always name the country, school and statute or authority behind a rule.
The main Sunni schools are Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali; Shi’a schools also exist.
Study sources and reasoning before applying rules to family, finance, crime or procedure.
Check current statutes and fatwas, and never issue a fatwa in an exam answer.

en.title: Introduction: Shari’ah, Fiqh and the Scope of Islamic Law
en.short: Shari’ah and fiqh, key terms, scope, variation by school and country, and study cautions.

sections.heading: Guidance and understanding
sections.text:
Shari’ah is the guidance revealed to the Prophet Muhammad in the Qur’an and Sunnah, his teachings and practice. Muslims regard it as the way God set out for belief, worship and conduct. Fiqh is the human effort by jurists to understand and apply that guidance in concrete situations. Fiqh is reasoned, organised in manuals and courts, and can differ between jurists. It is not itself revelation.

A useful distinction is between the source and the understanding. Shari’ah is the source and ideal; fiqh is the fallible human reading of it. A ruling in fiqh is therefore an opinion about what the guidance requires, not a direct quotation from God.

sections.heading: Scope and terms
sections.text:
Islamic law covers worship (ibadat) and transactions between people (muamalat). It includes family, inheritance, property, contracts, finance, crime, evidence and governance. Some rules are fixed and clear; others are open to interpretation. The course uses terms such as madhhab, a school of legal interpretation; mufti, a jurist who gives a non-binding opinion; fatwa, that opinion; and usul al-fiqh, the theory of how rules are derived. A qadi is a judge who decides cases.

Islamic law is not one uniform code. It is a family of legal traditions, and its place among legal systems differs. In Nigeria, for example, it operates within a plural system, mainly in personal status matters in northern states, and in twelve of them it also covers criminal matters; the exact courts and limits vary and should be checked.

sections.heading: Variation and example
sections.text:
Rules and their application vary by school, country and era. A Maliki jurist in West Africa, a Hanafi jurist in South Asia and a Shafi’i jurist in East Africa may answer the same question differently. State law may also codify one view or restrict another. This is why students should name the school, country and period when discussing a rule.

Example: Amina in Kano asks whether a particular sale is valid. A local mufti may answer from Maliki manuals and Nigerian state law. A jurist elsewhere might reach another view. The fatwa guides her conscience but is not a statute. These notes are study material, not legal advice; check the current official text and a qualified local lawyer.

keyPoints: Shari’ah is revealed guidance; fiqh is jurists’ reasoned understanding of it.
Fiqh is human and can differ between jurists, schools, countries and eras.
Islamic law covers ibadat and muamalat, including family, property, contracts and crime.
Madhhab means school of law; mufti gives a fatwa, a non-binding opinion; qadi is a judge.
Islamic law operates differently in different legal systems; in Nigeria it is mainly personal law in northern states, and in twelve of them it also covers criminal matters, with limits that vary.
These notes are study material, not legal advice; check current law and local authority.

en.title: Primary Sources: The Qur’an and the Sunnah
en.short: The Qur’an and Sunnah as primary sources, hadith transmission, authenticity and interpretation.

sections.heading: Qur’an as source
sections.text: The Qur’an is the book that Muslims believe God revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the Angel Jibril. In Islamic law it is the primary source and the measure of other sources. Its legal material is limited in quantity but foundational. Verses may be explicit in meaning (qat’i al-dalala) or open to more than one reading (zanni al-dalala). Jurists read commands, prohibitions, general and specific statements, and the reasons for revelation (asbab al-nuzul) when deriving rules. Tafsir is the discipline of interpreting the text.

sections.heading: Sunnah and hadith
sections.text: Sunnah is the Prophet’s normative practice: his sayings, actions and approvals. Hadith literature is the written record of reports about that practice. The two are related but not identical: a weak hadith may still be discussed by jurists, while Sunnah is the normative model, not every report. Hadith scholars examine the isnad (chain of transmitters) and the matn (text). Reports are classed as sahih (sound), hasan (good) or da’if (weak) in Sunni hadith science; Shi’a traditions use their own collections and criteria. A mutawatir report has so many chains that collusion is deemed impossible; an ahad report has fewer.

sections.heading: Deriving rules
sections.text: Jurists use the Qur’an and Sunnah together. A general Qur’anic command may be clarified by a hadith. For example, Qur’an 4:29 forbids consuming wealth unjustly and allows trade by mutual consent. A jurist asked about a new sale checks that verse, then hadith reports on consent, deception and uncertainty, then the school’s reasoning. The result is a legal opinion, not a direct quotation. Schools differ on how far a single-chain report can establish a rule and on which hadith collections they trust.

sections.heading: Interpretation and diversity
sections.text: Interpretation is not uniform. Jurists differ over literal and purposive readings, abrogation (naskh), and the weight of custom. Sunni and Shi’a traditions share the Qur’an but differ in hadith canon and in some doctrinal readings. A first-year student should learn the tools and the debates, not treat one school’s conclusion as the only possible reading.

keyPoints: The Qur’an is the highest primary source in Islamic law, and the Sunnah is the second primary source that explains and applies it.
Sunnah is the Prophet’s normative practice, while hadith literature is the record of reports about it.
Hadith scholars test reports through the isnad, the chain of transmitters, and the matn, the text.
A mutawatir report has many independent chains; an ahad report has fewer, and jurists differ on its legal weight.
Deriving a rule requires reading the text in context, checking related reports and interpretation, not quoting one verse alone.
Sunni and Shi’a traditions share the Qur’an but differ in hadith collections and some readings, so no single school’s reading is the only one.

en.title: Secondary Sources and Reasoning: Ijma, Qiyas and Ijtihad
en.short: Consensus, analogy and independent reasoning in Islamic law, their conditions and disputed scope.

sections.heading: Consensus (ijma)
sections.text: Ijma is the agreement of qualified jurists (mujtahids) of the Muslim community in a given era on a legal ruling. Classical theory usually requires that the agreement rest on a text or clear reasoning, that the jurists be competent, and that no equally qualified jurist dissent. Once settled, many jurists treat ijma as binding and as a source that can clarify or confirm the Qur’an and Sunnah, never contradict them. Disputes concern who counts as qualified, whether consensus must be universal or may be regional, whether silence gives consent, and whether later generations can overturn an earlier consensus. These are juristic doctrines, not one state’s statute; application varies by country and school.

sections.heading: Analogy (qiyas)
sections.text: Qiyas is extending a ruling from an original case (asl) in the texts to a new case (far') because both share an effective cause (illah). Conditions include a valid textual basis, an identifiable cause, a new case not already covered by stronger text, and a result that does not conflict with a clear rule. Example: the Qur’an forbids khamr (wine). If the cause is intoxication, jurists may extend the ban to another intoxicating drink. The Zahiri school and some others reject qiyas, while most Sunni schools accept it. Disputes also concern how the cause is identified and whether analogy can create new obligations.

sections.heading: Independent reasoning (ijtihad)
sections.text: Ijtihad is a qualified jurist’s total effort to derive a ruling from the sources. It includes qiyas but is wider. Conditions usually include mastery of Arabic, the Qur’an, Sunnah, abrogation, usul al-fiqh (the theory of the sources) and the aims of law. A jurist who meets them is a mujtahid. Disputes concern whether the gate of ijtihad closed, whether only collective bodies may practise it today, and how far it can depart from earlier schools. Schools reach different results because they weigh texts, causes and consensus differently. Check current official law where a state applies Islamic law.

keyPoints: Ijma is the agreement of qualified jurists in a given era on a legal ruling.
Classical theory treats ijma as binding when it rests on the texts and no qualified jurist dissents.
Qiyas extends a textual ruling to a new case through a shared effective cause (illah).
Most Sunni schools accept qiyas, but the Zahiri school and some others reject it.
Ijtihad is the qualified jurist’s effort to derive law, and qiyas is one of its tools.
Schools differ because they weigh texts, causes, consensus and the scope of reasoning differently.

en.title: Schools of Islamic Law: Formation and Diversity
en.short: The Sunni four and Ja’fari school: origins, methods, spread and ikhtilaf.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.text: A madhhab is a school of legal interpretation, not a separate religion. The main Sunni schools grew from teaching circles around four jurists in the eighth and ninth centuries CE: Abu Hanifa, Malik ibn Anas, al-Shafi’i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Their students preserved and developed their methods, so each school became a settled tradition. The Shi’a Ja’fari school takes its name from Ja’far al-Sadiq. Zaydi and Isma’ili traditions also survive. These schools share core beliefs but differ in legal reasoning.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: All schools accept the Qur’an and Sunnah as primary. Hanafis use qiyas (analogy) and istihsan (juristic preference) to avoid harsh results. Malikis give weight to the practice of Medina and maslaha (public welfare). Shafi’is set out a strict usul al-fiqh (principles of legal reasoning), limiting qiyas to clear cases. Hanbalis rely heavily on hadith and use qiyas narrowly. Most Ja’fari jurists today follow the Usuli approach, which adds 'aql (reason) alongside Qur’an, Sunnah and ijma (consensus). These differences produce varied answers, not different fundamentals.

sections.heading: Spread and ikhtilaf
sections.text: Today Hanafi law is common in Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia and South Asia. Maliki law is common in North and West Africa, including Nigeria. Shafi’i law is common in East Africa, Yemen and Southeast Asia. Hanbali law is common in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf. Ja’fari law is common in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain and Lebanon. Communities overlap, so check local practice. Ikhtilaf means legitimate disagreement among qualified jurists. It arises from different hadith, interpretation and custom. Schools are not ranked. Case: a Muslim in Kano, Nigeria, may follow Maliki law, while a Muslim in Istanbul, Turkey, may follow Hanafi law; each can regard the other’s position as ikhtilaf.

keyPoints: A madhhab is a school of legal interpretation, not a separate religion.
The four main Sunni schools are Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali, each named after a founding jurist.
The Shi’a Ja’fari school is named after Ja’far al-Sadiq, and Zaydi and Isma’ili traditions also survive.
The schools share the Qur’an and Sunnah but differ in their use of qiyas, istihsan, maslaha, local practice and 'aql.
Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i, Hanbali and Ja’fari law are associated with different regions, and communities overlap.
Ikhtilaf is legitimate disagreement among qualified jurists, not a ranking of schools.

en.title: Usul al-Fiqh: Legal Theory and Interpretation
en.short: How jurists read commands, ambiguity and conflict, and use ijtihad or taqlid to build rulings.

sections.heading: Rulings and language
sections.text: Usul al-fiqh is the theory of how rulings (ahkam) are derived from the sources of the law, chiefly the Qur’an and the Sunnah. A ruling (hukm) is the Lawgiver’s address concerning conduct. A command (amr) may indicate obligation or recommendation; a prohibition (nahy) may indicate prohibition or dislike. The context and an accompanying indicator (qarinah) decide. General words ('amm) may be restricted by specific words (khass). Absolute wording (mutlaq) may be qualified (muqayyad). A clear text (muhkam) is applied; an ambiguous one (mutashabih) is read with clear texts, and schools differ on how far reason may go.

sections.heading: Ambiguity and conflict
sections.text: When texts seem to conflict (ta’arud), jurists first try reconciliation (jam’). A conflict may be only apparent once context is known. If reconciliation fails, they consider abrogation (naskh), which requires reliable knowledge of chronology. They may then prefer one text (tarjih) by chain, wording or context. Example: a general command to honour parents is read with the specific prohibition on saying 'uff' to them (Qur’an 17:23). The specific text restricts the general; it does not cancel it. Schools order these steps differently.

sections.heading: Ijtihad and taqlid
sections.text: Ijtihad is a qualified jurist’s effort to reach a ruling. It requires knowledge of Arabic, the Qur’an, the Sunnah and related sciences. Taqlid is following a qualified jurist or school without independent derivation. For laypeople it is normal; scholars debate when ijtihad is required. Neither term is an insult: they describe methods and attitudes. A jurist may be right or wrong; the ruling is still an informed judgment.

sections.heading: Building an argument
sections.text: A usuli argument states the claim, cites the text, analyses its language, applies a principle, answers objections and concludes. It distinguishes certainty from probability. The conclusion is probable, not private opinion; the evidence must carry it. Modern statutes and courts vary by country, so check the current law.

keyPoints: Usul al-fiqh studies how rulings are derived from the sources of the law, not the detailed rules themselves.
A command or prohibition may imply obligation, recommendation, prohibition or dislike, depending on context and indicators.
General ('amm) and absolute (mutlaq) wording can be restricted or qualified by specific (khass) and qualified (muqayyad) texts.
When texts conflict, jurists try reconciliation, then abrogation, then preference (tarjih), though schools order these steps differently.
Ijtihad is independent effort by a qualified jurist; taqlid is following a qualified jurist or school.
A legal argument in usul al-fiqh moves from claim and text to linguistic analysis, principle, rebuttal and a probable conclusion.

en.title: Legal Maxims and the Objectives of the Law (Qawa’id and Maqasid)
en.short: How Islamic legal maxims and the maqasid, the higher objectives, guide jurists’ reasoning.

sections.heading: What a maxim is
sections.text: A qa’idah (plural qawa’id) is a short general statement that gathers many detailed rulings under one principle. Jurists use them to recall scattered rules and reason to new cases. A maxim is not a statute or a verse: it is a jurist’s summary with exceptions. The Ottoman Majalla, compiled between 1869 and 1876, opened with a list of them.

sections.heading: Leading maxims
sections.text: Common ones: al-umur bi-maqasidiha, matters are judged by their intentions; al-yaqin la yazul bi al-shakk, certainty is not displaced by doubt; al-darar yuzal, harm must be removed; la darar wa la dirar, harm may not be inflicted or returned; al-mashaqqah tajlib al-taysir, hardship brings ease, which allows concessions such as delaying a sick person’s fast; and al-'adah muhakkamah, custom is authoritative, including in reading contracts.

sections.heading: The maqasid
sections.text: Maqasid are the higher aims the law serves. Al-Ghazali (d. 1111) in al-Mustasfa and al-Shatibi (d. 1388) in al-Muwafaqat set out five necessities (daruriyyat): religion, life, intellect, lineage and property. Each is guarded by rules: life by the ban on killing, intellect by the ban on intoxicants, property by the ban on theft. Below necessities lie needs (hajiyyat) and refinements (tahsiniyyat). Some add honour; Ibn Ashur (d. 1973) added freedom and equality.

sections.heading: Reasoning and debate
sections.text:
The two work together: a maxim gives the shape of a rule, the maqasid explain why it exists. Amina in Kano, Nigeria, buys a sewing machine; a week later the motor fails. The sale is certain, so doubt about her consent does not undo it. But the defect is a harm, and harm must be removed, so she may return the machine and recover her money under the option of defect (khiyar al-'ayb). Protecting property is the aim behind both.

Most classical jurists treat maqasid as tools for reading texts, not a licence to set clear texts aside. Some modern scholars say they justify reform where texts are general or silent; others warn this lets a judge’s own views in.

keyPoints: A qa’idah is a general maxim drawn from many detailed rulings; it guides reasoning but is not a statute and has exceptions.
Certainty is not displaced by doubt: a proven sale or contract stands unless real evidence overturns it.
Harm must be removed, and harm may neither be inflicted nor returned.
Hardship brings ease, which is why the law allows concessions such as delaying a fast when sick.
The maqasid protect five necessities: religion, life, intellect, lineage and property, with needs and refinements below them.
Jurists disagree on scope: classical scholars use maqasid to read texts, while some modern scholars would use them to reform the law.

en.title: Historical Development of Islamic Law: Formative to Modern Periods
en.short: Formative, classical, colonial and modern Islamic legal history: schools, fiqh works, codification and reform.

sections.heading: Formative period
sections.text: Islamic law began with the Qur’an and the Prophet’s practice in seventh-century Arabia. After his death in 632, the community faced new questions. Early caliphs, judges (qadis) and scholars reasoned by analogy and local custom. Historians call this the formative period, but they date its end differently: some stop at the early Abbasid era, others later. Fiqh means the jurists’ understanding of the law, distinct from shari’ah, the revealed guidance.

sections.heading: Classical fiqh
sections.text: From the eighth to the tenth centuries, scholars collected hadith, debated method and wrote legal compendia. Schools (madhahib, singular madhhab) grew around teachers and students, not by decree. The Sunni Maliki, Hanafi, Shafi’i and Hanbali schools became dominant in different regions. Jurists practised ijtihad, independent reasoning, and later taqlid, following an established school. Some historians speak of a closing of the gate of ijtihad; others argue ijtihad continued. Works such as al-Shafi’i’s al-Umm and later manuals shaped teaching and judging.

sections.heading: Colonial period
sections.text: In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, European empires ruled much of the Muslim world. Colonial courts often applied Islamic law only in personal matters such as marriage and inheritance, while criminal and commercial law came from the coloniser. This varied by country. In British India, judges used translated fiqh texts, producing Anglo-Muhammadan law. In French Algeria, Islamic law was restricted and reorganised. In British Northern Nigeria, Islamic law continued in native and later Sharia courts under colonial supervision. Such arrangements helped fix rules that had been more flexible.

sections.heading: Codification and reform
sections.text: After independence, many Muslim-majority states codified parts of fiqh. Codification means putting rules into statute form. The Ottoman Mecelle, in the late nineteenth century, codified Hanafi contract law and influenced later codes. Modern states also reformed family law by statute, sometimes drawing on several schools. In Nigeria, Islamic personal law is applied in Sharia Courts of Appeal, whose jurisdiction is set by state law and the Constitution; check the current text. Historians disagree over whether these changes are renewal or departure.

keyPoints: Periodisation is a historian’s tool: the formative, classical, colonial and modern labels have no single agreed dates.
Fiqh grew through scholarly schools, with ijtihad (independent reasoning) and later taqlid (following a school) both present in practice.
Colonial rule usually confined Islamic law to personal matters and varied from one country to another.
Modern codification put selected fiqh rules into statutes, as the Ottoman Mecelle did for Hanafi contract law.
Family law reform by statute often draws on more than one school and differs by state.
For any current rule, check the statute, constitution or court decision of the country concerned.

en.title: Ibadat and Muamalat: Worship, Transactions and the Structure of Fiqh
en.short: Ibadat and muamalat in fiqh: examples, why law focuses on muamalat, and how worship shapes reasoning.

sections.heading: Two fields of fiqh
sections.text:
Fiqh is the human effort to work out practical rules of Islam. Jurists divide it into two broad fields. Ibadat (acts of worship) covers duties towards God: purification (taharah), the five daily prayers (salah), fasting (sawm), the alms due (zakat) and pilgrimage (hajj). Muamalat (transactions) covers relations between people: sale, lease, partnership, agency, marriage, divorce, inheritance, waqf and injury.

The division is a teaching device, not a wall. Classical manuals order the material more finely: worship, dealings, family law, inheritance, crimes, procedure. Some rules sit on the border. Marriage (nikah) is a contract with offer and acceptance, yet jurists also treat it as worship.

sections.heading: Why law studies muamalat
sections.text:
A law course concentrates on muamalat for practical reasons. Worship rules are mainly between the individual and God. A court does not normally hear a claim that someone prayed badly or missed a fast. Muamalat creates rights one person can claim against another, so it needs courts, evidence, remedies and, in modern states, statutes. Most modern codification of Islamic law has been in this field, especially family law and, more recently, finance.

Enforcement varies by country. Some states also police certain public aspects of worship; others leave worship to conscience. Check the law of the country you study.

sections.heading: Ritual rules and reasoning
sections.text:
Ritual rules still shape the system. Jurists grade every act on one scale of five rulings (al-ahkam al-khamsah): obligatory, recommended, neutral, disliked and forbidden. The same scale covers prayer and sale, and intention (niyyah) counts in both.

Zakat is the clearest bridge. It is worship, yet a wealth transfer with a rate and recipients. Suppose Amina’s savings stay above the nisab for one lunar year. The rate is 2.5 per cent, so 2,000,000 x 0.025 = 50,000 naira is due. The nisab is often given as about 85 grams of gold, but it varies; check current guidance.

Personal status shows the same overlap: marriage needs offer and acceptance, and witnesses in Sunni law, yet it is not a purely commercial bargain.

keyPoints: Fiqh divides into ibadat, duties towards God, and muamalat, relations between people.
Ibadat includes purification, prayer, fasting, zakat and hajj; muamalat includes sale, lease, partnership, marriage, inheritance and waqf.
Law courses focus on muamalat because those rules create enforceable claims and are the main subject of modern codification.
Courts normally do not enforce purely ritual duties, and enforcement of public worship varies by country.
The five rulings and the role of intention apply across both fields.
Zakat bridges the two: 2.5 per cent of savings held above the nisab for a lunar year, so 2,000,000 x 0.025 = 50,000 naira.

en.title: Legal Authority, Fatwa and the Role of Jurists
en.short: Fatwa versus qadi judgment, jurist qualifications and ethics, taqlid and modern fatwa councils.

sections.heading: Mufti and Qadi
sections.text:
A mufti is a scholar who issues a fatwa: a reasoned, non-binding opinion on a point of Islamic law. A qadi is a judge appointed by a state or court authority. A qadi’s judgment is binding and can be enforced; a fatwa guides conscience but does not by itself decide a dispute or transfer rights.

Suppose Amina in Kano, Nigeria, asks a mufti whether a sale is valid. The fatwa may advise her, but if the seller sues, a Sharia court qadi hears evidence and gives judgment under the law the court applies. The qadi’s order binds the parties; the mufti’s opinion does not.

sections.heading: Qualifications and Ethics
sections.text:
Qualifications differ by role. A mufti needs sound knowledge of the Qur’an, Sunnah, usul al-fiqh (legal theory), Arabic and the local context. A qadi needs legal training, appointment under the applicable law, and skill in procedure and evidence. Ethics for both include honesty, impartiality, avoiding conflict of interest and admitting uncertainty.

A mufti should not issue a fatwa without knowledge or for personal gain. A qadi must hear both sides and follow court rules. Limits follow from this: a mufti cannot enforce an opinion, and a qadi cannot decide simply by personal preference or outside the court’s jurisdiction. In many countries, qadis are bound by statute and appeal.

sections.heading: Taqlid and Councils
sections.text:
Taqlid means following a qualified scholar’s or school’s ruling without independently deriving it. It is normal for non-specialists; ijtihad is independent reasoning by a qualified jurist. Modern fatwa councils issue collective opinions. Examples include the OIC’s Islamic Fiqh Academy and Egypt’s Dar al-Ifta. Their authority varies.

In Saudi Arabia, the Permanent Committee for Islamic Research and Fatwas has an official role. In Nigeria, muftis and scholars advise, but Sharia courts decide cases. In some states, a fatwa may be given legal force by law; in others it remains advisory. Students should check the country’s current law and the council’s status.

keyPoints: A fatwa is a non-binding legal opinion; a qadi’s judgment is binding and enforceable.
A mufti needs knowledge of the sources and usul al-fiqh; a qadi needs appointment and procedural competence.
Both roles require honesty, impartiality and awareness of their limits.
Taqlid is following a qualified ruling without independent derivation; ijtihad is independent reasoning.
Modern fatwa councils issue collective opinions, but their legal force varies by country.
In Nigeria, fatwas generally advise while Sharia courts judge; check the current law.

en.title: Islamic Family Law: Marriage and Its Effects
en.short: Nikah elements, wali, mahr, witnesses, spousal rights, school differences and modern reforms.

sections.heading: Contract elements
sections.text: Nikah is the Islamic marriage contract. It is formed by offer and acceptance (ijab and qabul) between the parties or their representatives. Classical law requires the consent of both spouses, though schools differ on how a bride’s silence or guardian’s role is treated. The wali is the guardian who contracts a marriage for a bride in the Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali schools; the Hanafi school generally lets an adult woman contract for herself. Mahr is the dower, a sum or property promised to the wife; it is her right, not a price paid to her family. Sunni schools require witnesses (normally two), though details differ. Check the current family law of the country.

sections.heading: Effects and duties
sections.text: Marriage creates mutual rights and duties. The husband normally owes nafaqah, meaning maintenance such as food, clothing and housing according to his means. The wife keeps her own property and mahr. Both owe good treatment, fidelity and fair dealing. Classical schools differ on a wife’s duty of obedience, her freedom to work or travel, and polygyny. Polygyny is permitted in classical law with conditions of justice and maintenance, but many modern states restrict it. A concrete case: Amina, in Kano, Nigeria, marries Musa. Her father acts as wali, two witnesses attend, and mahr of 40,000 naira is agreed. The local Sharia court and state rules govern registration and any dispute.

sections.heading: Reform and practice
sections.text: Modern statutes often require registration, set a minimum age, protect consent, regulate polygyny and codify mahr. Morocco’s Moudawana 2004 and Tunisia’s Personal Status Code 1956 are well-known reforms, but their rules differ. In Nigeria, Islamic personal law is applied in Sharia courts in some states, and the applicable law varies by state. Do not assume one country’s rule applies elsewhere. This is study material, not legal advice. Always check the current statute, court rules and official guidance of the country concerned.

keyPoints: Nikah is a contract formed by offer and acceptance, with consent, mahr and witnesses.
The wali is required by Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali schools; Hanafi law generally allows an adult woman to contract herself.
Mahr is the wife’s dower and remains her property.
Nafaqah is the husband’s duty of maintenance according to his means.
Schools differ on obedience, travel, work and polygyny; modern statutes often restrict polygyny and require registration.
Family law is country-specific; check the current statute and court rules, especially in Nigeria where state law varies.

en.title: Islamic Family Law: Divorce, Maintenance and Custody
en.short: Divorce by talaq, khul' and court, iddah, maintenance, custody and child welfare in Islamic law and plural systems.

sections.heading: Divorce routes
sections.text: Talaq is divorce initiated by the husband. Classical Sunni law distinguishes a revocable talaq, where the husband may take the wife back during iddah, from an irrevocable one. A triple talaq in one sitting is debated: some classical jurists treated it as effective, while others and many modern statutes require one pronouncement at a time or court confirmation. Khul' is divorce initiated by the wife by agreement, usually returning mahr or paying compensation; schools differ on whether the husband’s consent or a court order is needed. Judicial divorce (faskh or tafriq) is granted by a court on grounds such as harm, desertion, non-maintenance or absence. Hanafi law is narrower; Maliki law is broader. Modern statutes vary widely.

sections.heading: Iddah and maintenance
sections.text: Iddah is the waiting period after divorce or the husband’s death. For divorce, the Qur’an sets three menstrual cycles (2:228); a pregnant woman waits until delivery (65:4); a widow waits four months and ten days (2:234). Maintenance (nafaqah) is the husband’s duty during marriage and during a revocable iddah; for an irrevocable iddah the schools differ. Amounts are not fixed universally; courts use need, custom and means. Check the applicable statute.

sections.heading: Custody and welfare
sections.text: Hadanah is custody, the day-to-day care of a child. It is not guardianship (wilayah) over property or marriage. Mothers usually have first custody, then female relatives, but schools differ on the age when custody ends and on the child’s choice. The governing principle is the child’s welfare (maslahah). Courts may transfer custody or order maintenance, schooling and contact.

sections.heading: Plural systems and safeguards
sections.text: Nigeria is a plural legal system. Islamic family law is applied mainly through Sharia Courts in states that have them, alongside statutory and customary courts; rules differ by state, so check the current state law and court rules. Safeguards include registration, notice, reconciliation under Qur’an 4:35, court permission where required, and a welfare report. Example: Amina seeks khul' in Kano. The court checks the contract, mahr, reconciliation and iddah under the law in force, not a textbook rule.

keyPoints: Talaq is husband-initiated divorce; khul' is wife-initiated by agreement; judicial divorce is granted by a court on stated grounds.
Iddah is the waiting period: three menstrual cycles after divorce, until delivery if pregnant, and four months ten days for a widow.
Maintenance (nafaqah) is generally the husband’s duty, but amount and duration depend on the school and the statute.
Hadanah is custody, not guardianship; the child’s welfare is the governing principle.
Schools and modern statutes differ, so always check the law of the country and state that applies.
Nigeria applies Islamic family law through state-based Sharia Courts within a plural system; rules vary by state.

en.title: Inheritance and Wills (Fara’id and Wasiyyah)
en.short: Fixed shares, residuaries, will limits and calculation under Islamic inheritance law.

sections.heading: Sources and heirs
sections.text:
Fara’id are fixed shares of inheritance set out in the Qur’an, mainly 4:11-12 and 4:176. They apply to close relatives such as spouse, children, parents and siblings.

A person may also make a wasiyyah, a will, but it is voluntary and operates after death. Classical manuals set out who inherits and who is excluded; Sunni schools and Twelver Shia law differ, so the relevant school and country matter.

sections.heading: Fixed shares and residuaries
sections.text:
After funeral costs, debts and any valid wasiyyah, fixed shares are calculated on what remains. Examples: husband 1/4 with a child, 1/2 without; wife 1/8 with a child, 1/4 without; mother 1/6 with a child or two or more siblings. A daughter alone may take 1/2, and two or more daughters 2/3 between them, when there is no son.

Residuaries (asabah) take the remainder. A son is a residuary and, with a daughter, takes twice her share. If shares exceed the estate, awl (proportional reduction) applies in Sunni law; Twelver Shia law differs. If residue remains, radd (return of residue) may give it to certain heirs, but schools differ.

sections.heading: Will and limits
sections.text:
A wasiyyah is limited to one-third of the net estate after debts. A bequest to an heir is generally invalid unless the other heirs consent, though schools differ. The will may appoint an executor and can cover non-heirs or charity.

Modern reforms in some countries, such as Egypt and Pakistan, give orphaned grandchildren a statutory share or obligatory bequest; details vary. Check the statute and court practice of the country where the estate is administered.

sections.heading: Calculation example
sections.text:
Example: estate after funeral and debts is 144,000. Heirs are wife, mother, son and daughter. Wife gets 1/8 = 18,000. Mother gets 1/6 = 24,000. Fixed shares total 42,000. Remainder is 102,000.

Son and daughter share it 2:1, so son gets 68,000 and daughter 34,000. Total: 18,000 + 24,000 + 68,000 + 34,000 = 144,000.

keyPoints: Fara’id are fixed Qur’anic shares; asabah are residuaries who take the remainder.
Fixed share = fraction × estate left after funeral costs, debts and a valid wasiyyah of at most one-third.
A son takes twice a daughter’s share when they inherit together as residuaries.
If fixed shares exceed the estate, awl scales them down in Sunni law; if residue remains, radd rules vary by school.
A bequest to an heir is generally invalid without the consent of the other heirs.
Sunni and Shia schemes differ, and modern statutes may add obligatory bequests; check the law of the relevant country.

en.title: Waqf and Endowment Law
en.short: Waqf creation, trustees, beneficiaries, perpetuity, revocation, trusts and modern regulation.

sections.heading: Definition and creation
sections.text: Waqf is the permanent dedication of defined property, or its usufruct, to God for a lawful purpose. The founder is the waqif, the property the mawquf, and the manager the mutawalli. Creation normally requires a clear declaration, defined property and a lawful purpose; some schools also require delivery of possession, and modern statutes often require registration. It may be public (khayri), for the poor or a school, or family (ahli), for named relatives. Example: Amina in Kano, Nigeria, declares a shop waqf for a Qur’an school and names her brother mutawalli; state law and the school of Islamic law govern registration and enforceability.

sections.heading: Trustees and beneficiaries
sections.text: The mutawalli is a trustee, not an owner. He must keep accounts, repair the property, invest prudently and pay income to beneficiaries. He cannot sell waqf property at will; a court or waqf authority may remove him for breach. Beneficiaries must be ascertainable. If a family waqf ends, income usually passes to charity. A trust also separates management from benefit, but the trustee holds legal title and beneficiaries equitable title. In waqf, ownership is often described as God’s, with people enjoying the usufruct.

sections.heading: Perpetuity and revocation
sections.text: Classical law treats waqf as perpetual and generally irrevocable once completed: the property cannot be inherited, gifted or sold. Many schools allow istibdal, exchange for other property, only where it benefits the waqf and a court or authority approves. Revocation before completion may be possible; after completion it is normally not. Schools differ, so the applicable school matters. Modern statutes may allow compulsory acquisition with compensation and may restrict family waqf.

sections.heading: Modern regulation and comparison
sections.text: Modern states regulate waqf differently. Egypt and Malaysia use ministries or state Islamic councils; Indonesia has a national waqf board; Nigeria depends on state law and Sharia courts. Current national or state law matters because it decides registration, land title, tax, court jurisdiction and removal of managers. Charitable endowments and trusts are comparable but not identical. Check the current official text for the country concerned.

keyPoints: Waqf is a permanent dedication of property or usufruct to God for a lawful purpose.
Creation needs a clear declaration, defined property and a lawful purpose; some schools also require delivery of possession, and modern statutes often require registration.
The mutawalli manages as a trustee, not an owner, and can be removed for breach.
Classical waqf is perpetual and generally irrevocable; istibdal is allowed only under strict conditions.
Waqf resembles a trust but differs on ownership and is governed by Islamic law and local statute.
Modern registration and supervision vary by country, so check the current national or state law.

en.title: Islamic Law of Contracts and Sale
en.short: Elements of a valid Islamic contract, sale, options, defects, gharar and exploitation.

sections.heading: Contract and sale
sections.text: An Islamic contract (aqd) is a binding tie created by offer (ijab) and acceptance (qabul). The parties must have capacity (ahliyyah), and consent (rida) must be genuine. The offer and acceptance should be clear and connected. A sale (bay') is the main example: an exchange of property for property by mutual consent. The seller transfers a thing or a described item, and the buyer pays a price (thaman).

sections.heading: Subject and price
sections.text: The subject matter (mahall) must be existing, owned by the seller, deliverable, known and lawful. The price must also be known. If an essential term is too uncertain, the sale suffers from gharar, excessive uncertainty, and is normally invalid. Small uncertainty that is unavoidable in ordinary trade is tolerated. Example: Amina offers to sell Musa a named bag of rice for ₦50,000 and he accepts. Object and price are known, so the core elements are present. If the rice is later found to have a hidden defect that was present at the sale, Musa may have the option of defect.

sections.heading: Options and defects
sections.text: Options (khiyar) let a party confirm or cancel. They include the session option before parting, the condition option agreed in the contract, the defect option for a hidden fault, and the inspection option after seeing the goods. Schools differ on which options apply and how long they last. Fraud (tadlis) and gross exploitation (ghubn fahish) may also give relief. Some schools allow rescission for a clearly unfair price; others require fraud or defect. The judge or statute may set limits.

sections.heading: Schools and codes
sections.text: The Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali schools agree on the core elements but differ on details, such as options and the effect of defects. Modern codes restate or adapt these rules. The Ottoman Majalla (1876) codified Hanafi contract rules. The UAE Civil Transactions Law (Federal Law No. 5 of 1985) includes contract provisions drawn partly from Islamic law. Other countries differ, so check the current statute and the school it follows.

keyPoints: A valid sale needs offer and acceptance, capable parties, genuine consent, a lawful and known subject, and a known price.
Gharar, excessive uncertainty in essential terms, normally invalidates a sale; minor uncertainty is tolerated.
Options (khiyar) allow cancellation or confirmation, including for defects, inspection, condition or the session.
Fraud (tadlis) and gross exploitation (ghubn fahish) may give relief, but schools differ.
Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali schools share core rules but differ on options and defects.
Modern codes such as the Ottoman Majalla and the UAE Civil Transactions Law adapt these rules; check current text.

en.title: Riba, Islamic Finance and Banking
en.short: Riba, gharar, maysir, Islamic finance structures, regulation and dispute resolution.

sections.heading: Prohibited elements
sections.text: Riba is an unjustified increase in a loan or exchange. The Qur’an condemns it (2:275-279). Jurists distinguish riba on loans from riba in sale, such as unequal exchange of the same commodity. Gharar is excessive uncertainty in a contract, for example selling an unknown or nonexistent thing. Maysir is gambling or gain by pure chance. Schools differ on where ordinary risk ends and prohibited gharar begins, so contracts are drafted to reduce uncertainty.

sections.heading: Main structures
sections.text: Murabaha is a cost-plus sale: the bank buys an asset and resells it at cost plus a disclosed profit, often paid in instalments. Mudarabah is a profit-sharing venture: one party supplies capital (rabb al-mal) and the other manages it (mudarib); profit is split as agreed, and loss falls on capital unless the manager is negligent. Musharakah is a joint partnership; profit is shared as agreed and loss in proportion to capital. Ijarah is a lease of an asset for rent, sometimes ending in ownership. Sukuk are certificates representing ownership of assets or usufruct, so returns come from the asset, not from interest.

sections.heading: Example and regulation
sections.text: Example: a bank buys a machine for 100,000 and sells it by murabaha for 110,000, a disclosed profit of 10,000. If repaid in 10 equal instalments, each is 11,000. This is a sale, not a loan. Regulation varies. Malaysia’s Islamic Financial Services Act 2013 governs Islamic banks supervised by Bank Negara Malaysia. In the UAE, the Central Bank of the UAE supervises Islamic banks. In Nigeria, the Central Bank of Nigeria licenses non-interest banks. Disputes may go to courts or arbitration; some countries have specialised commercial courts. Check current rules. This is academic, not financial advice.

keyPoints: Riba is a prohibited increase in loans or exchanges; gharar is excessive uncertainty; maysir is gambling.
Murabaha price = cost + disclosed profit; each instalment = price ÷ number of instalments.
Mudarabah profit is split by agreed ratio; loss falls on capital unless the manager is negligent.
Musharakah losses are shared in proportion to capital; ijarah leases an asset for rent.
Sukuk represent ownership in assets or usufruct, not interest-bearing debt.
Regulation and dispute resolution differ by country; check current law; these notes are academic, not financial advice.

en.title: Ownership, Property and Land Law
en.short: Property categories, ownership and possession, reviving dead land, pre-emption and leases in Islamic law.

sections.heading: Property and ownership
sections.text: In Islamic law, mal means property that has value and can be owned. Property may be movable or immovable, fungible (mithli, replaceable by weight or measure) or non-fungible (qimi). Ownership (milk) is the legal power over property. It can be complete, covering both the thing and its usufruct (manfa’ah), or incomplete, such as a lease that gives only use. Possession (yad) is factual control, and it is not the same as ownership. A person may hold property without owning it, as a trustee or tenant. Classical jurists distinguish owned property from unowned things (mubah), such as water or wild plants.

sections.heading: Reviving dead land
sections.text: Ihya al-mawat is the revival of dead land, land with no owner and no use. A hadith says that whoever revives dead land owns it. Jurists require that the land be truly dead, not public utility or already owned. Revival may be by clearing, digging a well, irrigating or building. Schools differ on whether the ruler’s permission is needed. Modern states often claim control of unallocated land. In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in the Governor of each state (and in the President for the Federal Capital Territory), so classical ihya must be read with statutory allocation.

sections.heading: Pre-emption and leases
sections.text: Shuf’ah is pre-emption: a right to take a property sold to a stranger on the same terms. It protects co-owners from an unwanted partner and neighbours from an unwanted neighbour. Schools differ on who holds it: some limit it to co-owners in undivided property, others extend it to certain neighbours. Some modern statutes in the Middle East and North Africa codify shuf’ah, but courts often restrict it. Ijarah is a lease: the sale of usufruct for a rent. The rent, term and maintenance duties must be clear. Example: Amina in Kano clears dead land and irrigates it. Under classical ihya she may own it, but the Land Use Act 1978 requires statutory allocation. If a co-owner later sells, a neighbour may claim shuf’ah in some schools, not all. Always check the local land statute and court practice.

keyPoints: Mal is property; milk is ownership; yad is factual possession, which is not the same as ownership.
Ihya al-mawat revives unowned dead land, but modern states such as Nigeria regulate land through statutes.
Shuf’ah is a right of pre-emption for co-owners or certain neighbours, and the schools differ on its scope.
Ijarah is a lease of usufruct for rent, and the rent, term and maintenance duties must be clear.
Nigeria’s Land Use Act 1978 vests land in state governors (Federal Capital Territory land vests in the President), so classical rules must be read with statutory allocation.
Codification of shuf’ah and land rules varies by country, so always check the local statute and court practice.

en.title: Islamic Criminal Law: Hudud, Qisas and Ta’zir
en.short: The three offence categories, strict hudud evidence, qisas, ta’zir and modern debates.

sections.heading: Three categories
sections.text: Classical fiqh groups offences into hudud, qisas and ta’zir. Hudud are fixed penalties described as claims of God, for offences such as theft, highway robbery, zina (unlawful sex), qadhf (false accusation of zina) and drinking alcohol. Schools differ on the list and on apostasy. Qisas is retaliation for homicide or injury, available to the victim or heirs. Ta’zir is discretionary punishment for other wrongs. Boundaries overlap, and jurists classify some acts differently.

sections.heading: Evidence and doubt
sections.text: Strict proof is central to hudud. A hadd is not imposed where there is shubha, meaning doubt or ambiguity. Zina classically requires four witnesses to the act, or confession; schools differ on details. Theft requires proof of ownership, a minimum value and taking from safekeeping; thresholds vary. Confession must be voluntary and may be retracted. These rules make conviction rare in classical doctrine. Qisas and ta’zir use different standards.

sections.heading: Qisas and ta’zir
sections.text:
Qisas covers intentional killing and injury. Victims or heirs may demand retaliation, accept diya (compensation), or forgive; the state need not compel retaliation. Ta’zir lets a judge or ruler punish acts that threaten public order or morality. Modern states often codify ta’zir offences in detail, more than they codify hudud.

Suppose Amina in Kano, Nigeria, is accused of stealing a phone. With no confession and one witness, hadd theft is not proved under classical rules. A court might consider ta’zir if the penal code allows, but the current statute must be checked.

sections.heading: Modern application
sections.text:
Application is limited and varies greatly. Saudi Arabia and Iran apply hudud; Pakistan has hudud laws but practice has changed; Sudan and several northern Nigerian states have Sharia penal codes, though in Nigeria appeal courts have overturned some convictions. Brunei introduced a Sharia penal code in stages. Other Muslim-majority states mostly use ta’zir and ordinary codes.

Rights bodies criticise corporal and capital punishments, unequal treatment and privacy. Reformers urge procedural safeguards, codification, moratoria or reading hudud through maqasid (the higher objectives of Islamic law). Defenders argue strict evidence and forgiveness protect defendants. These are contested; check current law.

keyPoints: Hudud are fixed penalties for specified offences, but schools differ on their list and scope.
A hadd is not imposed where there is shubha, meaning doubt or ambiguity.
Qisas permits retaliation or diya for homicide or injury, and forgiveness is possible.
Ta’zir is discretionary punishment for wrongs outside hudud and qisas.
Modern application varies by country, so check the current statute and court practice.
Debates over corporal and capital punishment, equality and privacy remain contested.

en.title: Evidence and Procedure in Islamic Courts
en.short: Proof rules (witnesses, oaths, documents) and the qadi’s procedure in classical and modern courts.

sections.heading: Burden of proof
sections.text:
Classical doctrine puts the burden of proof (bayyinah) on the claimant and the oath (yamin) on the defendant who denies, following a well known hadith that proof is for the one who claims and the oath for the one who denies. Bayyinah is wider than testimony: it means whatever establishes the right.

Example: Amina claims Bashir owes ₦200,000 for goods. She must produce the written contract or witnesses. If she produces nothing, Bashir may swear, and the claim normally fails.

sections.heading: Witnesses and oaths
sections.text: Testimony (shahadah) must come from an adult, sane witness of good character ('adalah) speaking from direct knowledge. Numbers vary by subject and school: two male witnesses for most financial matters, one man and two women in some cases under Qur’an 2:282, and four witnesses for zina. Schools differ on whether a non-Muslim may testify against a Muslim. Oaths are sworn in God’s name; a defendant who swears is generally released.

sections.heading: Documents and other proof
sections.text: Qur’an 2:282 orders that debts be written down, and classical jurists accepted written documents, often requiring witnesses or proof of authenticity. A confession (iqrar) by a person of full capacity binds that person. Modern courts also receive expert evidence, records and circumstantial proof, though schools differ on the weight of circumstantial evidence.

sections.heading: The qadi’s procedure
sections.text: The qadi hears the claimant, then the defendant, treats both equally in seating and speech, and may urge settlement (sulh). The general rule is that judgment rests on the evidence presented; schools differ on whether the judge’s own knowledge may also count. Today procedure is governed mainly by national statute, not by fiqh alone: Nigeria’s Sharia Courts of Appeal sit under the 1999 Constitution, with state laws governing Sharia criminal courts in the north; Malaysia has codified Syariah court procedure; other countries have their own rules. Check the current statute and court rules of the country concerned.

keyPoints: The claimant bears the burden of proof; a defendant who denies may take an oath.
Bayyinah means any proof that establishes the right, not only oral testimony.
Witness numbers vary: two men for most financial matters, four for zina; schools differ on details.
A valid confession (iqrar) binds the person who makes it.
The qadi hears both sides equally and may encourage sulh before judgment.
Court procedure today is set by national statute; check the current rules of the relevant country.

en.title: Islamic Constitutional and Administrative Thought: Siyasah Shar’iyyah
en.short: Classical caliphate and imamate theories, shura, justice, obedience, public interest and siyasah shar’iyyah.

sections.heading: Caliphate and imamate
sections.text: Classical Sunni jurists called the political office the caliphate (khilafah) or imamate (imamah). Al-Mawardi, in Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya, and Abu Ya’la described the ruler’s duties: protect religion, defend territory, appoint officials, collect taxes and give justice. The ruler had to be Muslim, male, just, capable and of Quraysh descent according to many classical texts, though qualifications varied. Sunni theory allowed selection by consultation or by designation, and later by force followed by allegiance. Shia Imami theory treats the imam as divinely appointed and sinless; Twelver Shia await the hidden imam. These are ideal theories, not a single historical constitution.

sections.heading: Shura, justice, obedience
sections.text: Shura means consultation. Qur’an 3:159 and 42:38 commend it, but classical jurists disagreed whether the ruler’s consultation was binding or advisory. Justice ('adl) is a central duty; a ruler who rules unjustly may lose legitimacy, though jurists differed on rebellion. Obedience (ta’ah) is owed in lawful matters; a command to sin is not obeyed. Public interest (maslahah) lets rulers act for welfare where texts are silent, provided no clear rule is broken.

sections.heading: Siyasah shar’iyyah
sections.text: Siyasah shar’iyyah means governance according to Shari’ah. It covers discretionary administrative measures by the ruler or judge for public welfare, such as price control, market regulation or appointing officials. Ibn Taymiyyah’s al-Siyasa al-Shar’iyya argued that justice and trust (amanah) are essential, and that rulers and subjects must cooperate in lawful good. The doctrine is not a licence to ignore clear texts; jurists set limits.

sections.heading: Modern arrangements
sections.text: Modern states differ. Constitutions, parliaments, elections, courts and separation of powers are not classical institutions. Some Muslim-majority states, such as Saudi Arabia under its 1992 Basic Law, declare the Qur’an and Sunnah their constitution; Iran’s 1979 Constitution combines elected bodies with clerical guardianship; Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution does not adopt a state religion (section 10), and Islamic law applies in some northern states, covering personal status and, since 2000, also criminal matters. Historical practice differed: dynastic succession, sultanates and colonial rule often departed from classical theory. Check each country’s current constitution and statutes.

keyPoints: Classical Sunni theory calls the office caliphate or imamate and lists duties such as justice, defence and appointment of officials.
Shura is consultation, and jurists disagreed on whether the ruler must follow its advice.
Obedience is due only in lawful matters, and justice is a condition of legitimate rule.
Siyasah shar’iyyah is discretionary governance for public welfare within the limits of Shari’ah.
Modern constitutions, parliaments and courts are not classical institutions, and Muslim-majority states arrange them differently.
Historical practice often differed from theory, so check each country’s current constitution and statutes.

en.title: Islamic Law and Human Rights: Dignity, Duties and Disagreement
en.short: Dignity, rights and duties in Islamic law, and debates on religion, women and punishment.

sections.heading: Dignity, rights, duties
sections.text: Karama means dignity, the honour Islamic texts attribute to every human being. Haqq is a right or claim; taklif is legal duty. Jurists often pair huquq Allah, claims owed to God, with huquq al-ibad, claims owed to people. Rights and duties are usually correlative: a wife’s maintenance right is a husband’s duty. Scholars disagree whether rights or duties come first in Islamic legal reasoning.

sections.heading: Freedom of religion
sections.text: The Qur’an states 'no compulsion in religion' (2:256), and many jurists read it as protecting inward belief. Classical schools nevertheless differed on apostasy: some treated it as a capital offence, others stressed persuasion or distinguished belief from public order. Modern scholars and Muslim-majority states disagree, and national laws on apostasy and blasphemy vary. ICCPR article 18 and UDHR article 18 protect freedom of religion, with limited restrictions. Check each state’s current law and reservations.

sections.heading: Women and punishment
sections.text: Debates on women’s rights concern qiwama (maintenance and authority), inheritance shares, testimony and divorce. Schools and modern reformers differ. CEDAW article 16 requires equal marriage rights; several Muslim-majority states entered reservations, often citing Shari’ah. Corporal punishment debates concern hudud (fixed penalties) and qisas (retaliation). ICCPR article 7 and the Torture Convention 1984 prohibit cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment. Some states apply such penalties, others do not; jurists argue over strict proof, doubt (shubha) and proportionality.

sections.heading: Comparing standards
sections.text: International standards include the UDHR 1948, ICCPR and ICESCR 1966, CEDAW 1979 and the African Charter 1981. The Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam 1990, adopted by the OIC, presents an Islamic framework and subordinates all its rights to Shari’ah; it is a declaration, not a binding treaty. Scholars disagree whether these systems are compatible, complementary or in tension. Many modern scholars argue from maqasid, the higher aims of the law, such as justice and dignity. Enforcement and reservations vary by state.

keyPoints: Karama is dignity, haqq is a right or claim, and taklif is duty; jurists distinguish claims owed to God (huquq Allah) from claims owed to people (huquq al-ibad).
Qur’an 2:256 says there is no compulsion in religion, but classical and modern views on apostasy and blasphemy law differ, and national laws vary.
Women’s rights debates include qiwama, inheritance, testimony and divorce; CEDAW article 16 has attracted reservations from several Muslim-majority states.
Corporal punishment debates set hudud and qisas against ICCPR article 7 and the Torture Convention 1984, with disagreement over proof, doubt and proportionality.
The Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam 1990 is an OIC declaration, not a binding treaty, and subordinates all its rights to Shari’ah.
Schools, scholars and states disagree on these issues, so check the current national law and each treaty’s reservations.

en.title: Islamic International Law (Siyar)
en.short: Classical rules on war, peace, treaties, prisoners and non-Muslims, and their modern relevance.

sections.heading: What siyar covers
sections.text:
Siyar is the fiqh branch on relations between the Muslim polity and others: war, peace, treaties, prisoners, safe conduct and non-Muslims under Muslim rule. Siyar is the plural of sirah, meaning conduct or course.

The split between dar al-Islam (territory of Islam) and dar al-harb (territory of war) is a juristic classification, not a Qur’anic phrase; some jurists added dar al-sulh, land bound by treaty. The earliest systematic text is Kitab al-Siyar by the Hanafi jurist al-Shaybani (d. 805 CE).

sections.heading: War and its limits
sections.text:
Classical manuals limit fighting to combatants. Women, children, the elderly and monks should not be killed; treachery, mutilation and the killing of envoys are forbidden; crops and fruit trees are generally spared. These rules are often traced to instructions attributed to Abu Bakr.

On prisoners, Qur’an 47:4 allows release freely or by ransom, and jurists debated ransom, exchange, enslavement or release, with the ruler choosing. Declaring war belonged to the ruler, not to private persons.

sections.heading: Peace and non-Muslims
sections.text:
Peace is made by sulh (agreement) or hudna (armistice). The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, a ten-year truce with the Quraysh of Mecca in 628 CE, is the model; jurists differed on the maximum term, many taking ten years as a guide.

Aman is safe conduct making an enemy a musta’min, temporarily protected. A well-known report says even an ordinary Muslim, including a woman, could grant it. Dhimmis are non-Muslim subjects who keep their religion and internal law, pay jizya, a tax, and are excused military service; the ruler set the amount.

sections.heading: Modern relevance
sections.text:
Most Muslim-majority states are parties to the UN Charter and the Geneva Conventions, and modern relations run through territorial states, not the abode division. Contemporary jurists disagree: some treat the classical rules as historically conditioned and argue that peace is the default; others hold them binding.

No worldwide body legislates siyar, so practice varies by country. Check the law of the state concerned.

keyPoints: Siyar is the fiqh of war and peace, developed by jurists rather than by statute or treaty.
Dar al-Islam and dar al-harb are juristic categories, not Qur’anic terms.
Classical rules protect non-combatants and forbid treachery, mutilation and killing envoys.
Aman gives an enemy temporary protection as a musta’min; dhimmis pay jizya and keep their religion.
The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah is the main precedent for truces, and jurists differed on their maximum length.
Modern state practice and the UN Charter differ from classical doctrine, and jurists disagree on how to reconcile them.

en.title: Islamic Law in Nigeria: Courts, Jurisdiction and Application
en.short: Sharia courts in Nigeria: history, personal law, constitutional limits and state variation.

sections.heading: Background and structure
sections.text: Nigeria is a plural legal system: English-derived law, customary law and Islamic law operate together. Islamic law was applied in the northern emirates before colonial rule. Colonial rule preserved Islamic courts in the north while limiting their reach. After independence, the Constitution and state laws shaped them. The 1999 Constitution provides for a Sharia Court of Appeal of the Federal Capital Territory (sections 260 to 262) and for a Sharia Court of Appeal in any state that requires one (sections 275 to 277). Below these appellate courts, states use Sharia courts or Area Courts, and their names and powers differ.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction
sections.text: The Constitution’s Sharia Court of Appeal jurisdiction is civil, not general criminal. It covers questions of Islamic personal law, such as marriage, divorce, maintenance, custody, guardianship and inheritance, in defined cases, usually where the parties are Muslims or the matter concerns a Muslim marriage, will, waqf (an Islamic endowment) or succession. It does not make Islamic law the general law of Nigeria. From 1999 onwards, several northern states enacted Sharia penal codes and gave Sharia courts criminal jurisdiction. Those extensions are politically and constitutionally contested. Non-Muslims are not generally bound by Islamic personal law, and freedom of religion is protected in section 38.

sections.heading: State variation and example
sections.text: Practice varies by state and over time, so check the current constitution, state statutes and court decisions. Suppose Aisha and Musa, Muslims in Kano State, divorce and dispute custody. Their case may be heard in the state Sharia court system because it concerns Islamic personal law. If the same couple disputes a commercial contract, the ordinary High Court is the usual forum. If one party is not Muslim, the Sharia court’s personal-law jurisdiction may not apply; the state law and the facts must be checked. This is an illustration, not legal advice.

keyPoints: Nigeria has a plural legal system in which Islamic law mainly applies as personal law.
The 1999 Constitution provides for Sharia Courts of Appeal for the Federal Capital Territory and for states that require them.
The Constitution’s Sharia Court of Appeal jurisdiction is civil Islamic personal law, not general criminal law.
Several northern states extended Sharia courts into criminal matters from 1999 onwards; this is contested.
Court names, powers and practice vary by state and change over time.
Always check the current constitution, statutes and court decisions; these notes are not legal advice.

en.title: Legal Pluralism and Comparative Islamic Law
en.short: This summary covers Islamic law in plural legal systems, codification, and comparative method across Africa and Asia.

sections.heading: Plural systems
sections.text: Legal pluralism means one state recognises more than one body of law. Islamic law may be state law, personal law for Muslims, or unofficial practice. In Nigeria, Islamic personal law is applied by Sharia courts in many northern states alongside common law, statute and customary law; jurisdiction varies by state. In Malaysia, civil courts and Syariah courts coexist, and Syariah courts handle personal law for Muslims under state enactments. Indonesia mixes a civil-law heritage, Islamic courts and adat (customary) law. These systems differ, so name the country and forum.

sections.heading: Codification
sections.text: Codification puts rules into a statute or code. It changes classical fiqh because the state selects among school opinions, fixes procedure and gives courts authority. The Ottoman Mecelle (1869-1876) codified Hanafi rules on transactions. Egypt and Tunisia codified parts of personal status in the twentieth century, drawing selectively on classical rules. A code may narrow or freeze rules that jurists once debated, so always check the current text.

sections.heading: Comparative method
sections.text: Comparative study should not treat one school or country as the norm. Ask: what is the legal question, which forum has jurisdiction, which school or statute applies, and what historical context shaped it? Distinguish official law, living practice and classical doctrine. A functional comparison can help, but translated terms such as 'custody' may not match classical concepts. State the limits of your comparison.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Amina, a Muslim in Kano, seeks divorce. A Sharia court may apply Maliki law as received in Nigeria and affected by state law; related custody or maintenance may involve civil statute. The student should identify jurisdiction, the applicable school and statute, and whether codification changed classical options. She should not assume Egyptian Hanafi rules apply.

keyPoints: Legal pluralism means one state recognises more than one body of law, so Islamic law may apply through state courts, personal-law statutes or custom.
In Nigeria, Sharia courts apply Islamic personal law in many northern states alongside common law, statute and customary law; jurisdiction varies by state.
Malaysia has civil courts and Syariah courts, with Syariah jurisdiction over Muslims set by state enactments.
Codification selects among classical opinions and fixes procedure, as the Ottoman Mecelle did for Hanafi transactions.
Comparative method must name the country, forum, school and statute, and avoid treating one tradition as the norm.
Distinguish official codified law, living practice and classical fiqh when comparing.

en.title: Ethics, Adab and Professional Conduct in Islamic Law
en.short: Adab of jurists, qadis and lawyers, compared with modern professional codes and enforceable rules.

sections.heading: Meaning of adab
sections.text: Adab means disciplined conduct and character, not mere etiquette. In Islamic legal ethics it covers the duties of the jurist (faqih), the mufti who issues fatwas (legal opinions), the qadi who judges, and the lawyer who represents clients. The Qur’an commands that trusts be returned and that people be judged justly (4:58), and that believers stand firm for justice (5:8). Classical manuals on adab al-qadi (judicial conduct) treat these as duties: truthfulness, competence and restraint.

sections.heading: The qadi’s duties
sections.text: Classical adab requires a qadi to be competent, impartial, patient and accessible. A qadi should hear both parties, treat them equally in speech and seating, decide only on evidence, and avoid gifts, loans or private meetings with one litigant. A judgment given through bias or without hearing the other side is defective. The qadi should refuse a case if there is a close relationship with a party, and should not sit while angry or distracted. These rules protect confidence and access to justice.

sections.heading: Jurists and lawyers
sections.text: A mufti must answer honestly, know the facts and the applicable school, and say when the matter is uncertain. A jurist must not issue a fatwa to favour anyone, and payment must not shape the opinion. A lawyer must be competent, keep confidences, avoid conflicts of interest and not mislead the court. Suppose Amina, a lawyer in Kano, finds that her client has sworn a false affidavit. Nigerian professional conduct rules require her not to present false evidence; she should advise correction and, if the client refuses, may need to withdraw.

sections.heading: Modern codes
sections.text: Modern professional codes share these ideals: honesty, competence, confidentiality, impartiality and access to justice, often through legal aid or pro bono work. But adab is mainly a religious and ethical standard. Enforceable duties come from national law and the relevant bar or law society. In Nigeria, the Legal Practitioners Act and the Rules of Professional Conduct for Legal Practitioners 2007 set duties, and the Legal Practitioners Disciplinary Committee hears complaints. Check the current statute and rules.

keyPoints: Adab in Islamic law means disciplined professional character, not mere etiquette.
A qadi must be competent, impartial, hear both sides and avoid gifts or private contacts with litigants.
A mufti or jurist must be honest and competent, and must not let favour or payment shape a fatwa.
Modern professional codes share these ideals but make them enforceable through national law and bar rules.
In Nigeria, the Legal Practitioners Act and the Rules of Professional Conduct for Legal Practitioners 2007 provide enforceable duties; check the current text.
Access to justice requires courts and lawyers to be accessible and to treat all parties fairly.

en.title: Codification, Reform and the Modern State
en.short: How Muslim-majority states codify fiqh, reform family and finance law, and justify change through siyasah and maqasid.

sections.heading: Codification and the Mecelle
sections.text: Codification means putting legal rules into a written code enacted by the state. The Ottoman Mecelle (Majalla), prepared between 1869 and 1876, codified Hanafi rules on contracts and civil transactions. It showed that a state could turn fiqh into statute, but it covered muamalat, not worship. Classical fiqh remained a jurists’ law, so codification shifted authority toward the legislature.

sections.heading: Family law reform
sections.text: Family law was reformed more slowly. Egypt’s personal status laws of 1920 and 1929 kept a Hanafi base but adopted rules from other schools to protect women. Tunisia’s Code of Personal Status 1956 prohibited polygamy and made divorce a matter for courts. Morocco’s 2004 Family Code used maqasid, the objectives of Shari’ah, to justify reforms such as raising the marriage age. States often use takhayyur, choosing an opinion from another school, or talfiq, combining parts of different rulings. These reforms are often justified by maslahah, public interest.

sections.heading: Siyasah, maqasid and finance
sections.text: Siyasah shar’iyyah is the ruler’s discretionary power to govern for public welfare within Shari’ah. States cite it and maqasid to regulate Islamic finance. Malaysia’s Islamic Financial Services Act 2013 and Nigeria’s central bank rules for non-interest banking are examples. These laws set licensing, capital and disclosure standards. The state thus sets standards that classical fiqh did not contain. Critics ask whether such rules are fiqh or state policy.

sections.heading: Authority and caution
sections.text: The tension is real. Classical jurists claimed interpretive authority; modern legislatures claim democratic legitimacy. A state may select a ruling that classical scholars disputed, so the result is law, not necessarily the majority fiqh view. Statutes also change. Different countries have different rules, and courts may interpret them differently. Check the current official text for any country before relying on a rule. This summary is for study, not legal advice.

keyPoints: Codification turns fiqh into state statute, as the Ottoman Mecelle did for Hanafi civil transactions.
Family law reforms in Egypt, Tunisia and Morocco used takhayyur, talfiq and maqasid to change classical rules.
Siyasah shar’iyyah gives the state discretion to govern for public welfare within Shari’ah.
Islamic finance laws in Malaysia and Nigeria show state regulation beyond classical fiqh.
State legislation may select a disputed opinion, so it is law but not necessarily majority fiqh.
Statutes change by country and year; check the current official text before relying on a rule.

en.title: Advanced Usul al-Fiqh, Maqasid and Contemporary Ijtihad
en.short: Advanced usul, maslahah, maqasid, collective ijtihad and the arguments on legal renewal.

sections.heading: Reading usul critically
sections.text:
