Advanced usul al-fiqh studies how a jurist moves from text to ruling. It examines commands and prohibitions, literal and figurative meaning, general and specific wording, and unqualified and qualified terms.

Read a primary text such as al-Ghazali’s al-Mustasfa or al-Shatibi’s al-Muwafaqat by separating the author’s text, examples and assumptions. Ask what problem the rule answers and which school it serves. Read a modern fatwa, a jurist’s opinion, the same way: identify the question, sources, reasoning and authority.

sections.heading: Maslahah and maqasid
sections.text:
Maslahah means a benefit or the averting of harm. Al-Ghazali allowed it only under strict conditions, often summarised as necessity, certainty and generality. Al-Shatibi placed it within maqasid al-shariah, the objectives of the law.

These are commonly listed as religion, life, intellect, lineage and property; some add honour. They are ranked as necessities, needs and embellishments. Maqasid can guide interpretation, but it can be used loosely. The critical question is whether a claimed benefit is real, public and consistent with clear texts.

sections.heading: Collective ijtihad
sections.text:
Ijtihad is the jurist’s effort to derive a ruling from the sources. Collective ijtihad (ijtihad jama’i) means consultation among specialists, as in a fatwa council. It can pool expertise in medicine, economics and law. It is not infallible, and its decisions are opinions unless a state gives them legal force, which varies by country.

A small case: a fatwa body in Kano, Nigeria, is asked about a new administrative rule. It should state the facts, check for clear text, weigh maslahah, record dissent and explain its method publicly.

sections.heading: Renewal debate
sections.text:
Arguments for legal renewal stress that texts are fixed but circumstances change. They appeal to maqasid, maslahah and the avoidance of hardship. Arguments against warn that renewal can become subjectivism, reading modern preferences into revelation.

They also point to the shortage of qualified jurists and the value of stability and precedent. The debate is best judged by method: who decides, what evidence is used, how dissent is treated and whether reasons are public.

keyPoints: Usul al-fiqh is a method for deriving rulings, not a list of rulings.
Maslahah is a benefit or averting of harm; al-Ghazali set strict conditions for it.
Maqasid al-shariah are the objectives of the law, commonly ranked as necessities, needs and embellishments.
Collective ijtihad pools specialist opinion but is not infallible or automatically binding.
A fatwa is generally an opinion; its legal force depends on the state, so check national law.
The renewal debate turns on method: evidence, authority, dissent and public reasoning.

en.title: Islamic Finance Law and Regulation: Contracts, Markets and Supervision
en.short: Advanced Islamic finance contracts, sukuk, takaful, supervision, accounting and dispute resolution.

sections.heading: Contracts and structures
sections.text:
Advanced Islamic finance uses named contracts to reach stated economic aims. Murabaha is cost plus disclosed profit. Ijara is leasing. Musharaka is partnership, mudaraba is profit-sharing between capital and work, and wakala is agency. Salam and istisna cover deferred delivery and manufacture. Each contract has its own rules on risk, ownership and price.

Example: a bank buys an asset for 100,000 and sells it to a customer for 105,000 payable in five equal instalments of 21,000. The 5,000 is disclosed profit, not interest. The bank must own the asset and bear ownership risk before sale.

sections.heading: Sukuk and takaful
sections.text:
Sukuk are certificates of equal value representing undivided ownership in assets, usufruct (the right to use and take benefit from property) or projects. Common structures include ijara, murabaha and musharaka. Some are asset-backed; many are asset-based, so investors rely on the originator’s credit.

Takaful is cooperative insurance. Participants contribute to a tabarru (donation) fund that pays claims; surplus and deficits are handled under the scheme rules. Retakaful is reinsurance for takaful. Wording and capital treatment vary by jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Regulation and accounting
sections.text:
Supervision differs. Malaysia has a dedicated Islamic financial services law, the Islamic Financial Services Act 2013, and a central bank Shariah Advisory Council. The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Nigeria supervise Islamic banks and windows through their central banks under general or non-interest banking rules. Check each current law, licence type, capital and liquidity rule.

AAOIFI, the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions, issues accounting and Shariah standards; IFSB, the Islamic Financial Services Board, issues prudential standards. Adoption is not uniform. Shariah boards, internal Shariah review and audit form Shariah governance.

sections.heading: Disputes and comparison
sections.text: Disputes may go to civil or commercial courts, arbitration or mediation. Courts may need Shariah expert evidence, and the binding force of a Shariah board ruling varies. Compare jurisdictions by legal basis, supervisor, Shariah governance, insolvency and enforcement. Do not assume one model travels. Rules and standards change, so check the current official text and the country’s regulator. This is study material, not legal advice.

keyPoints: Murabaha is cost plus disclosed profit; the bank must own and bear risk before sale.
Sukuk represent ownership in assets or usufruct, but asset-based sukuk often carry originator credit risk.
Takaful pools contributions in a tabarru fund to pay claims, with surplus rules set by the scheme.
Malaysia has a dedicated Islamic finance statute, IFSA 2013; other named states supervise through central bank rules.
AAOIFI and IFSB standards are influential but adopted unevenly.
Dispute forums and the binding effect of Shariah rulings vary, so check current law.

en.title: Islamic Law and Biomedical Ethics
en.short: Usul and maqasid applied to abortion, assisted reproduction, organ donation and end-of-life care.

sections.heading: Method and terms
sections.text: Usul al-fiqh is the theory of how rules are derived from the Qur’an, Sunnah, ijma (consensus) and qiyas (analogy). Maqasid al-shariah are the law’s objectives, classically five: religion, life, intellect, lineage and property; some modern scholars add others, such as dignity. In bioethics, jurists weigh texts against these objectives, using maslahah (public interest) and darurah (necessity). A fatwa is a scholar’s opinion; it is not a statute. The result is a range of views, not one rule.

sections.heading: Abortion and reproduction
sections.text: On abortion, classical jurists differed. Many allowed it before ensoulment (nafkh al-ruh, when the soul is breathed into the foetus) for a serious reason, but the timing and conditions vary; some forbade it from conception. Modern scholars also differ. Assisted reproduction: most Sunni jurists permit IVF using the husband’s sperm and wife’s egg during marriage, but reject donor gametes and surrogacy because they confuse nasab (lineage). Some Shia jurists allow limited donor arrangements. Example: a couple in Kano use IVF with their own gametes; most jurists regard this as permitted, while donor sperm would be rejected by most Sunni schools.

sections.heading: Organs and end of life
sections.text: Organ transplantation is widely permitted by contemporary scholars if there is consent, no sale of organs, no serious harm to the donor, and just allocation. Cadaveric donation is accepted by many, but brain death is contested; some accept it, others require circulatory death. End-of-life care: active euthanasia and suicide are prohibited. Withholding futile treatment and giving pain relief are generally allowed, provided ordinary care continues. A case: a brain-dead patient’s family asks about kidney donation; a scholar may permit it under a state donation law, but another may refuse on brain-death grounds.

sections.heading: Law and advice
sections.text: Positive law and clinical regulation differ by country. Nigeria, for example, regulates abortion mainly through criminal law with narrow exceptions, and several countries, including some Muslim-majority states, have organ-donation statutes. Always check the current statute, hospital policy and professional code. This summary is academic, not medical or legal advice.

keyPoints: Usul al-fiqh supplies the method; maqasid supply the objectives used in Islamic bioethics.
Abortion positions vary by school and stage of pregnancy, especially before or after ensoulment.
Most Sunni jurists allow IVF with the couple’s own gametes but reject donor gametes and surrogacy.
Organ donation is widely permitted with consent and justice, though brain death remains contested.
Active euthanasia is prohibited; withholding futile treatment and palliative relief are generally allowed.
Positive law and clinical rules differ by country, so check current official sources; this is academic only.

en.title: Research Methods and Dissertation in Islamic Law
en.short: Framing questions, using fiqh texts, fatwas, statutes and cases, and writing a dissertation responsibly.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text: A dissertation needs a narrow, answerable legal question. Start with a puzzle, not a topic. Example: Amina, a student in Kano, Nigeria, studies Islamic finance disputes. A weak topic is 'Islamic finance in Nigeria'. A workable question is: 'How have Nigerian Sharia courts reasoned about murabaha disputes in reported cases since 2010?' Murabaha is a sale at a disclosed mark-up. She must define it, choose dates, identify courts and state her method. If no reported cases exist, revise the question, not invent data.

sections.heading: Sources and criticism
sections.text: Distinguish primary from secondary sources. The Qur’an and Sunnah are primary religious sources. Fiqh manuals and fatwa collections are secondary religious sources; statutes and law reports are positive legal sources. Read a classical fiqh text in a critical edition and note its madhhab (school), genre and date. A fatwa is an opinion, not a statute, unless a state gives it legal force. Check the mufti, question, date and jurisdiction. For statutes and cases, use official gazettes, consolidated texts and authorised reports. In Nigeria, a dissertation on a State Sharia Court of Appeal must check the 1999 Constitution, State law and amendments, not an old textbook.

sections.heading: Methods and ethics
sections.text: Textual method means close reading in the original language where possible, checking terms, translations and context. Comparative method compares like with like: explain each country’s history, courts and statute before concluding. Avoid transplanting a rule without its context. Research ethics include honest quotation, accurate citation, confidentiality, consent for interviews and no plagiarism. Discuss religious texts and schools of thought respectfully and report differences fairly.

sections.heading: Writing and citation
sections.text: A dissertation usually has an introduction, literature review, methodology, chapters, conclusion and bibliography. Use one citation style. For a fiqh text, give author, title, editor, publisher, year, volume and page. For a fatwa, give the collection, mufti, date and fatwa number. For a case, give court, year, volume, reporter and page. For a statute, give country, title and year. Verify every current legal rule with the official source, because law changes by country and year.

keyPoints: A good dissertation question names the jurisdiction, period, sources and method.
Classical fiqh texts must be read in critical editions with their school, genre and date noted.
A fatwa is an opinion, not binding law unless the state gives it legal force.
Statutes and cases must be checked in official current texts and authorised reports.
Comparative work must explain context before comparing; textual work must check language and translation.
Cite every source consistently and verify every current legal rule with the official source.
